units.title: 1. Connect the chapter into one reasoning process

blocks.text: Try each question before opening its explanation. For a missed question, identify whether the difficulty was translation, truth evaluation, witness scope, or proof structure, then return to the corresponding lesson.

rows: Read connectives, truth values, and conditional language.
Translate specifications and puzzles into an explicit logical model.
Rewrite equivalent formulas and test satisfiability.
Track domains, scope, and single quantifiers.
Track quantifier order and dependent witnesses.
Build a valid argument or give a countermodel.
Write a direct, contrapositive, contradiction, or equivalence proof.
Use exhaustive cases, existence, uniqueness, symmetry, and invariants.

blocks.text: The chapter moves from sentences to formulas, from formulas to valid deductions, and from deductions to proofs. The practice here uses original examples across that whole sequence.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between a conjecture and a theorem?

explanation.text: A conjecture is proposed as true but has not been established. A theorem has a proof based on its mathematical assumptions. Many examples can motivate a conjecture without turning it into a theorem.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 2. Retrieve the truth rules without guessing from English

blocks.text: Let p mean “the sensor is active” and q mean “the log is open.” OR is inclusive unless explicitly stated otherwise. A programming command that changes the log is an action; the proposition “the log is open” is true or false.

blocks.prompt: If the sensor is inactive and the log is closed, is p → q false?

explanation.text: No. Here p = F and q = F, so the conditional is true. The single false row for implication is p = T and q = F. This does not claim a cause-and-effect relationship.

blocks.prompt: Classify p ∨ ¬p, p ∧ ¬p, and p → q.

explanation.text: The first is a tautology, the second a contradiction, and the third a contingency: its value varies with the assignment. Negation flips a proposition’s truth value.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 3. Translate only if, unless, and exactly one

blocks.text: Let e mean “entry is allowed,” b mean “a badge is valid,” and g mean “a guest pass is valid.” Interpret the rule as a fictional access specification.

rows: Entry is allowed only if a badge is valid.
A valid badge is sufficient for entry.
Entry is forbidden unless a guest pass is valid.
Exactly one of badge and guest pass is valid.

blocks.prompt: Give the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of e → b. Which is equivalent to the original?

explanation.text: Converse: b → e. Inverse: ¬e → ¬b. Contrapositive: ¬b → ¬e. Only the contrapositive is always equivalent to the original; the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other.

blocks.prompt: Does “Entry is forbidden unless a guest pass is valid” promise entry to every pass holder?

explanation.text: No. It says a valid guest pass is necessary for entry: e → g. It does not supply g → e. Other conditions may still prevent entry.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.
Simplify ¬(p → q) ∨ (p ∧ q). Try a law-based derivation before checking a table.
Equivalence means the expressions agree on every assignment, not merely one satisfying row. A truth table can independently verify this two-variable derivation.

blocks.prompt: Are p → q and ¬p → ¬q equivalent?

explanation.text: No. Take p = F and q = T. Then p → q is true while ¬p → ¬q is false. This single differing row disproves equivalence.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 5. Check whether a specification can be satisfied

blocks.text: Let u mean “upload starts,” c mean “connection is available,” and m mean “maintenance is active.” Require u → c, m → ¬c, and m. These rules alone do not require an upload.

blocks.prompt: Give a satisfying assignment and a justified conclusion.

explanation.text: u = F, c = F, m = T satisfies all three requirements. From m and m → ¬c infer ¬c; then from u → c and ¬c infer ¬u. Thus the rules force no upload, but are consistent.

blocks.prompt: What happens if u is added as a fourth requirement?

explanation.text: The system becomes inconsistent. From u → c and u obtain c, but the maintenance premises already give ¬c. No assignment satisfies all four requirements.

blocks.text: Two fictional people are each either always truthful or always lying. Ada says “Ben is truthful.” Ben says “Ada and I are different types.” Let a and b mean that Ada and Ben are truthful. Require a ↔ b and b ↔ (a ⊕ b). The only model is a = F, b = F. Both statements are then false, consistent with both speakers being liars.
A satisfiable model establishes logical consistency under the supplied rules. It does not establish that the fictional rules accurately describe any real person or system.
Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 6. Build a formula from the true rows

blocks.text: Disjunctive normal form, or DNF, is an OR of AND terms. For each true row of a Boolean function, form an AND term that is true exactly on that row, then OR those terms together.

blocks.description: The two true rows produce a formula for the biconditional.

blocks.text: This construction shows that AND, OR, and NOT can express every finite Boolean truth table. If no rows are true, use a contradiction such as p ∧ ¬p. “Functionally complete” means a collection of connectives can express every such Boolean function.

NAND, written p ↑ q, means ¬(p ∧ q). It alone is functionally complete: NOT p is p ↑ p; p AND q is (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q); p OR q is (p ↑ p) ↑ (q ↑ q). These replacements give gates for the same truth behavior.

blocks.prompt: Why does a DNF row term contain ¬p when that row has p = F?

explanation.text: The literal must be true on the selected row. If p is false, ¬p is true. Using p instead would select the wrong assignments.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 7. Keep the domain and eligibility condition visible

blocks.text: Let the domain be employees in a specified office. T(x) means x is trained and A(x) means x has access.

rows: Not every trained employee has access.

blocks.prompt: Negate “Some trained employee has access” and explain the result.

explanation.text: ¬∃x (T(x) ∧ A(x)) is equivalent to ∀x (¬T(x) ∨ ¬A(x)), or ∀x (T(x) → ¬A(x)). It says no employee has both properties. It does not say no employees are trained.

blocks.prompt: If the employee domain is empty, which of the four table statements are true?

explanation.text: The first and third universal statements are true. The second and fourth existential statements are false. Do not infer existence from a universal claim without a nonempty-domain assumption.

blocks.prompt: In (∀x P(x)) ∨ Q(x), which occurrences of x are bound?

explanation.text: The x inside P(x) is bound by ∀x. The x in Q(x) is free. The parentheses stop the quantifier’s scope before the OR.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 8. Test whether one witness must serve everyone

blocks.text: Let R(s, t) mean student s reviewed topic t. Students are Ana and Bo; topics are Logic and Proofs.

blocks.prompt: Negate ∀s ∃t R(s, t), keeping negations next to predicates.

explanation.text: The negation is ∃s ∀t ¬R(s, t): some student reviewed no topic. Flip each quantifier in order and negate the predicate. The student appears before the topic because the original order is preserved.

blocks.prompt: Write: every student reviewed some topic in every chapter. Use R(s, t) and In(t, c).

explanation.text: With s over students, c over chapters, and t over topics: ∀s ∀c ∃t (In(t, c) ∧ R(s, t)). The topic may depend on both the student and the chapter. Moving ∃t to the front would demand one topic for all those choices.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 9. Trace a valid deduction and expose an invalid one

blocks.text: Suppose p → q, q → r, and ¬r. Prove ¬p without a full truth table.

blocks.prompt: If the third premise were r instead of ¬r, would p follow?

explanation.text: No. Set p = F, q = F, r = T. Both implications and r are true, but p is false. Reversing the chain without justification affirms its conclusion.

blocks.prompt: All calibrated sensors are tested, and all tested sensors are logged. Sensor d is not logged. What follows?

explanation.text: Instantiate both universal rules at the same sensor d. Not logged implies not tested by modus tollens; not tested then implies not calibrated. The domain must include d.

blocks.prompt: Some sensor is calibrated and some sensor is logged. Must one sensor be both?

explanation.text: No. The two existential witnesses may differ. Use two sensors, one calibrated only and the other logged only, as a countermodel.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 10. Write complete proofs with integer witnesses

blocks.prompt: Prove directly that the product of two odd integers is odd.

explanation.text: Let m = 2a + 1 and n = 2b + 1, with integers a and b. Then mn = 4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1. The expression 2ab + a + b is an integer, so mn is odd.

blocks.prompt: Prove by contraposition: if n² is even, then n is even.

explanation.text: For integer n, suppose n is not even, so n = 2k + 1 for an integer k. Then n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 is odd, hence not even. This proves the contrapositive and therefore the original implication.

blocks.prompt: Prove: if r is rational and t is irrational, then t − r is irrational.

explanation.text: Suppose for contradiction that s = t − r is rational. Then t = s + r is rational: if s = a/b and r = c/d with nonzero integer denominators, s + r = (ad + bc)/(bd), a rational number. This contradicts t being irrational.

blocks.prompt: Does either direction alone prove that n is even if and only if n² is even?

explanation.text: No. The reverse implication was proved above. The forward implication also needs justification: n = 2k gives n² = 2(2k²), which is even. Together the two directions prove the biconditional.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 11. Practice cases, existence, uniqueness, and obstruction

blocks.prompt: Prove |x| = |−x| for every real x using cases.

explanation.text: If x ≥ 0, then |x| = x and |−x| = x. If x < 0, then |x| = −x and |−x| = −x. The cases cover every real number, including zero.

blocks.prompt: Find the unique real solution of 3x − 2 = 10 and prove both obligations.

explanation.text: Existence: x = 4 gives 3·4 − 2 = 10. Uniqueness: if y also solves it, subtract to get 3(y − 4) = 0, so y = 4.

blocks.prompt: A board has 10 dark squares and 12 light squares. Every legal tile covers one of each. Can it be tiled?

explanation.text: No. Any number of such tiles covers equal counts of the two colors. The unequal counts are an obstruction independent of how you place the tiles.

blocks.prompt: What is wrong with proving x² > 0 by checking only x > 0 and x < 0?

explanation.text: The real domain also contains zero, where x² = 0. The two cases are not exhaustive, and the claimed strict inequality is false at the omitted point.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.

units.title: 12. Build a truth-table and bit-operation checker

blocks.text: Project: implement AND, OR, XOR, implication, and biconditional on Boolean inputs. The following small JavaScript functions provide a starting point. Treat their input contract seriously: p and q must be Boolean values, and bit strings must be nonempty, equally long strings of 0 and 1.

blocks.description: Executable JavaScript. String operations preserve leading zeros and avoid fixed-width numeric bitwise coercion.

blocks.text: Deliver a four-row Boolean table, tests for all pairs of short bit strings, and rejected-input tests. Extension: represent formulas as a small expression tree, enumerate all 2ᵏ assignments for k variables, and return a satisfying assignment or report that none exists. Do not equate one failed assignment with unsatisfiability.

blocks.prompt: How would you extend this to the common fuzzy AND/OR convention?

explanation.text: For values in [0, 1], use min for AND and max for OR, explicitly labeling that convention. For 0.3 and 0.8, the outputs are 0.3 and 0.8. This is a different model from ordinary Boolean logic; do not silently mix the two.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Computer Projects, printed page 119.

units.title: 13. Explore games and tilings with verifiable search

blocks.text: Game project: encode a Chomp board as nonincreasing row lengths, with poison at the first square of the first row. A safe move at (r, c) shortens every row i ≥ r to min(oldLength[i], c), using zero-based coordinates. Skip the poison move. The position [1] is losing; any position with a safe move to a losing position is winning. Cache repeated positions.

blocks.prompt: Evaluate the small boards [1], [2], [2, 1], and [2, 2].

explanation.text: [1] is losing. [2] is winning because its safe move leaves [1]. [2, 1] is losing because either safe move leaves a two-cookie line, which is winning. [2, 2] is winning because removing its bottom-right cookie leaves [2, 1].

blocks.text: Tiling project: store the remaining board squares. Choose the first uncovered square and try every allowed tile placement covering it. Reject overlaps and out-of-board squares; recurse on the remaining squares. An empty board is success. If every legal placement fails, report failure. Record actual placements so another program can check the result.

Exploration extensions: search for integers with two unordered square-sum representations; generate small polyominoes and identify shapes under translation, rotation, and reflection; compare area and color obstructions with exhaustive tiling results. State bounds and duplicate rules explicitly.

blocks.prompt: What must accompany a reported tiling?

explanation.text: A list of tile placements and a separate check that each tile has an allowed shape, lies on the board, and covers each required square exactly once. A picture or a “success” message alone is weaker evidence.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Computer Projects and Computations and Explorations, printed page 119.

units.title: 14. Explain a model and audit a proof

blocks.text: Choose one short writing project. State the precise question, define the terms, include a small worked example, and cite the sources you actually use. Keep a theorem, an experimental result, and a conjecture clearly distinguished.

rows: Model a scheduling or puzzle constraint with satisfiability.
Define variables, encode at-least-one and at-most-one constraints, and exhibit a model or explain a contradiction.
State the selected fuzzy operators, compute a numerical example, and explain what the values mean.
Audit a flawed proof or a logical paradox.
Identify the earliest unjustified inference or inconsistent modeling assumption; repair it if possible.
Investigate Prolog, resolution, or automated proof.
Show a tiny example, explain what the system establishes, and separate proof search from proof checking.
Explain a game or tiling argument.
Specify legal moves or tile shapes, prove the key invariant or strategy, and state its limitations.

blocks.prompt: How would you encode exactly one of three choices a, b, c?

explanation.text: Use (a ∨ b ∨ c) ∧ (¬a ∨ ¬b) ∧ (¬a ∨ ¬c) ∧ (¬b ∨ ¬c). The first clause requires a choice; the other three forbid every pair from being selected together. Omitting the first clause permits none.

blocks.text: When writing about the current state of an open problem or a software tool, verify it with a dated primary source. A textbook’s historical description or a search experiment is not automatically current evidence.
Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Writing Projects, printed page 120.

units.title: 15. Run a final self-check before sets and functions

blocks.title: You are ready to move on when…

blocks.text: You can translate a statement with its domain, negate it without changing its meaning, tell whether witnesses may differ, justify an inference, and write a short proof whose assumptions and conclusion are explicit.

blocks.prompt: A team claims: “Every student has solved some problem, so some problem was solved by everyone.” What is the error?

explanation.text: It swaps ∀s∃p for ∃p∀s. Ana solving only A and Bo solving only B is a countermodel. Each student has a witness, but there is no shared witness.

blocks.prompt: A proof says two hypothetical solutions must be equal. Has it established exactly one solution?

explanation.text: It has established at most one. It still needs existence, either by giving a valid solution or by another existence argument.

blocks.prompt: A program checked every input in its documented finite domain and found a property true. Is that merely sampling?

explanation.text: If coverage, the implementation, and the interpretation of the property are justified, it is exhaustive verification for that finite domain. It says nothing automatically about inputs outside that domain.

blocks.text: Chapter 2 reuses this language for sets, functions, sequences, and matrices. Membership statements become predicates; set identities become equivalences; claims about functions require quantifiers and proofs. Keep the domain-and-witness habits from this chapter.
Textbook connection: Chapter 1 Key Terms and Results, Review Questions, and Supplementary Exercises, printed pages 115–119.
